title: Stability vs Momentum — candidate riff for SRE-Senior
content:
Purpose: informal scratch to separate two axes I keep confusing when evaluating senior infra candidates: long-term stability (will they stay, scale org knowledge, steward systems) vs recent momentum (new wins, energetic upskilling, bold shipping). Intended for my own passback to the hiring slate and to seed a short debrief with the panel.

Context: candidate = "Ryan Cho" (applied for Senior SRE / runtime infra). Interview loop: two system-designs, one on-call simulation, one culture/soft-skills. Interviewers: Diego (runtime), Maya (SRE), Evan (serving runtime).

Quick gut framing (not final):
- Stability: medium-low. Signals: 4 companies in 5 years; two contract roles in 2023–24; strong ownership stories but often short tenure.
- Momentum: high. Signals: recent project at last role moved a production cache system from 97% to 99.8% reliability, shipped automations that removed 2 FTE of toil, good energy in whiteboard.

Why this matters: Senior roles here require both — steady ownership (custodial thinking, handoffs, runbooks) and the ability to push new optimizations without breaking everything. Candidate may be a net positive if we accept slightly higher retention risk in exchange for near-term throughput gains on infra debt.

Stability vs Momentum matrix (quick heuristics):
- Anchor signals (stability): tenure > 2 yrs at a major employer; ownership of a long-lived service; on-call rota membership over >12 months; codebase authorship with long-tail followups.
- Momentum signals: recent measurable product wins; fast prototyping; leading migrations; public blog posts or talks in past year.
- Negative flags: pattern of leaving after single-sprint wins; contract-heavy CV without depth; avoidance of operational tedium in answers (e.g., "we had oncall but I never paged").

Candidate scoring (my provisional):
- Technical depth: 7/10 — good mental models, answered KV cache tradeoffs well, sketchy on kernel-level perf tuning (fine for role).
- System design: 8/10 — clear partitioning, strong failure-mode analysis.
- Operational maturity: 5/10 — runbooks existed but maintenance story fuzzy, handoff calibration light.
- Team fit / communication: 8/10 — clear, accountable, good with feedback.
- Retention risk: 4/10 (higher risk).

Net: recommend a focused follow-up to probe stability levers before moving to offer band. If follow-up reassures (concrete tenure commitments or management context), tilt to green.

Suggested follow-up asks (short take-home / 30-min follow-up):
1) Walk me through a long-lived incident you owned end-to-end where the postmortem forced a multi-month change (org/process/tech). I want dates, stakeholders, and the maintenance plan.
2) Show a commit history example where you followed up on an initial implementation with a performance regression found >6 months later. How did you notice? What changed?
3) How do you think about tradeoffs between shipping a migration now vs deferring and absorbing technical debt? Give a concrete decision you led and the 6–12 month outcome.

Red flags to listen for in follow-up: vague timelines, conflating "I set it up" with "I maintained it", inability to name oncall partners/stakeholders, no evidence of addressing long-tailed bugs.

Compensating positives to weigh:
- Plays well with product/infra tradeoffs, would likely move several medium-term initiatives quickly (cache tuning, rollout pipeline improvements).
- Good mentorship instincts observed in pair session.
- Clear bias for automation and measurable impact (we have tickets that map to this pattern).

Decision options (what I'd pass to hiring committee):
- Option A (conservative): pass to team with ask: second loop focused on long-term ownership. If follow-up is ok, proceed to final loop with hiring manager.
- Option B (aggressive): proceed to manager loop and salary negotiation now, accept higher retention risk because of immediate runway needs on infra debt.
- Option C (reject): if follow-up shows pattern of one-off migrations and lack of maintenance, reject.

My preferred route: Option A. Low-effort follow-up that should disambiguate the biggest risk.

Immediate next steps (for me):
- Draft 3 follow-up prompts and send to Diego to own the 30-min check (diego@redwood).
- Add a short 'maintenance evidence' field to our scorecard template so we force interviewers to capture concrete dates/links.
- Mark candidate as "hold — follow-up" in the tracker (JIRA-RUN-4532).

Notes-to-self (misc, scribbles):
- Candidate mentioned "we rotated oncall weekly" — check whether that meant full ownership or just paging.
- Great analogies using cache coherence examples — useful for future interview question wording.
- Ask Maya to paste the pair-session snippet where candidate debated cache eviction policies — strong signal of system-level intuition.

Unresolved / hypothesis to validate:
- Hypothesis: candidate's short tenures are due to intentional rotations to gain breadth, not instability. Validate via dates and manager feedback.
- Hypothesis: candidate will commit to multi-year tenure if the role offers ownership of a stable system + product roadmap clarity.

Tone: keep this document light and private — personal riff not intended as final hiring record. Will transcribe the outcomes of the follow-up into the canonical scorecard if we move forward.

End.
